supports_claims: 4x4 E/N grid with forbidden P(1,2),Q(3,2) yields 19 avoiding paths.

conventions.statement: A shortest route on the lattice uses only unit East and North moves.
S=(0,0), T=(4,4) for target; the 4x4 diagram includes all grid vertices.
Avoiding a checkpoint means never visiting its vertex, although a path can visit two checkpoints.
Distinct ordered E/N words are distinct paths.

teaching_path.action: On a fresh small grid, count paths via a fixed marked vertex as a product of independent prefix and suffix counts.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Subtract the two forbidden checkpoint counts independently with no add-back.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: On a small lattice with U(1,1) and V(2,2), can one E/N route pass through both?
misconceptions.repair: A route visiting both is removed once for each forbidden set. Restore paths through both by counting three consecutive segments.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Any two forbidden vertices can lie on the same monotone path.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Can an E/N path visit (1,2) and (2,1) in either order without moving backward?
misconceptions.repair: The two marker coordinates must be comparable componentwise; otherwise the intersection is empty.

predict.prompt: On a 2x2 E/N grid can one shortest path pass two marked vertices? Draw an example and explain when the order is possible.
predict.defensible_answer: Yes for an ordered pair, such as U(1,0) then V(1,1); no when one mark is northeast in x but southwest in y.

boundary_test.prompt: In a 3x3 E/N grid with U(1,1) and V(2,2), a student calculates 20-12-12 and calls this final. Explain why that is impossible, count through-both and correct it.
boundary_test.answer: Twenty total, 12 through each; eight through both (2×2×2). Avoid both 20-12-12+8=4; direct subtract-only is negative.
boundary_test.confirms: Fix double subtraction of paths belonging to both forbidden families.

questions.stem: In a 4-by-4 square lattice, S=(0,0) to T=(4,4), a shortest path uses only East and North unit edges. Two vertices are forbidden: P=(1,2) and Q=(3,2). How many shortest paths avoid BOTH? Construct and use a representation of paths through each marked vertex; decide from the diagram whether a path may visit both, and justify the total. A bare binomial calculation is insufficient.
conditions: Forbidden vertices may lie on one shared route; determine this yourself.
Original authored TEST, no official source provenance.

answer.summary: 19 shortest E/N paths avoid both P(1,2) and Q(3,2).
reasoning: P is southwest of Q, so shared E/N paths exist. S->P 3 routes, P->Q 1 (two East), Q->T 3, yielding 9 through BOTH.
answer.check: Independent exhaustive enumeration over all 70 E/N words confirms 19 avoid both and 9 visit both.

reasoning_route.action: Map target grid to 70 E/N words, and through-P and through-Q families.
reasoning_route.why_valid: Four E/four N give C(8,4); one marker splits path counts.

reasoning_route.action: Recognize order-comparable marker geometry, build three-segment path through both and correct double-removal.
reasoning_route.why_valid: S->P->Q->T monotone, so shared path count3×1×3=9; inclusion-exclusion restores it.

reasoning_route.action: Enumerate 70 words independently and filter visits.
reasoning_route.why_valid: Exactly 19 fail to visit either mark.
